payload.rationale: I estimate an 18% chance that the CDC-reported United States measles count for 2026 exceeds 6,000 under the contract’s expiration and revision rules. No current case counts or outbreak reports were supplied, so this is a broad background-based estimate, not a projection from observed 2026 incidence. For historical scale, the substantial 2019 US outbreak year recorded roughly 1,280 cases. Exceeding 6,000 would require a considerably larger national burden, likely involving sustained transmission across multiple undervaccinated communities. High population immunity and outbreak-control measures weigh against that outcome, while clustered susceptibility, repeated introductions, and potentially accelerating transmission leave a meaningful upper-tail risk. The strongest reason this estimate could be too high is that transmission may remain concentrated and successfully contained, with the actual September count already making the threshold remote. The strongest reason it could be too low is that declining local vaccination coverage may already have produced large, connected outbreaks in 2026; without the year-to-date count, I cannot recognize that possibility. Settlement depends on the qualifying CDC count available under the frozen rules, not an eventual revised estimate of infections.
limitations: No supplied evidence on 2026 year-to-date cases, outbreak geography, vaccination coverage, or transmission trends.
Historical outbreak experience may transfer poorly if susceptible populations and outbreak connectivity have changed.
No browsing or tools were available to verify current CDC reporting.
Reporting delays and exclusion of post-expiration revisions could affect settlement near the threshold.
